description: We are Team Heat Sync, a two-person team in the Philadelphia NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We chose the event Flame in Freefall to understand how smoke behaves in space and what that means for the detectors astronauts rely on. We built Silent Alarm to help people explore NASA’s experiments, check the sources behind each finding, and see which questions still need testing.
summary: Silent Alarm is a research tool for fire safety in space, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 Flame in Freefall Challenge. A smoke detector is only useful if it sounds. In NASA's SAME experiment on the ISS, under the conditions studied, the tested smoke detector would have stayed below its alarm threshold in around two-thirds of Teflon smoke experiments and over half of Kapton smoke experiments. Silent Alarm makes this research significantly easier to find and harder to misread. A browser-based model ranks the 9 NASA fire research studies by how well they all relate to the user's question, and an AI-generated summary explains the top 3. Each sentence in an AI response must reference a NASA record, and any sentence that does not reference a source is automatically deleted. If its records do not cover a question, Silent Alarm states that explicitly rather than fabricating information. An evidence gap map shows where smoke detectors have been studied (which materials and under specific conditions) and where they have not. Each gap, including every Moon and Mars gravity case, is turned into a suggested future experiment. Overall, Silent Alarm shows what has been learned, and what remains to be learned, about smoke detectors as astronauts gear up for missions to the Moon and Mars.
details:
What it does

Silent Alarm is a website that enables fire safety researchers to discover and view evidence of smoke detectors from NASA. The website includes the following:

1. Investigations: Researchers input a question, and a small AI model executed within the browser ranks nine combustion investigations in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database. Based on the model’s assessment, a summary is provided for the top three investigations. Each sentence in the summary is linked to the original NASA PSI database entry for that investigation.

2. Detector Evidence: Based on NASA’s SAME experiment on the ISS, this page details what evidence was discovered regarding smoke detectors for Kapton and Teflon. Each piece of evidence is also explained regarding its test conditions, source, and limitations.

3. Smoke Analysis: This page features a graph detailing how smoke particles developed after aging for 720 seconds using data from the SAME Final Science Report for four different materials. Researchers can also input their own questions regarding the smoke detector evidence.

4. Evidence Gap Map: This section displays a grid linking different materials to gravity levels (Mars, Moon, and ISS) to illustrate both the presence and absence of evidence. Each identified gap is also linked to a suggested experiment that would provide that evidence.

How it works

Built using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, this website is deployed using AWS Amplify. Using Transformers.js to execute MiniLM sentence embeddings within the browser (without sending the input question to any external database), the available information is ranked against questions. Responses are generated using Groq’s gpt-oss-120b model via an AWS Lambda function to ensure the API key is never sent to the browser. Each request to the model is limited to NASA data only; each sentence in the response must be linked to a data source, any sentences not linked to a source are removed, and responses that reference data not provided to the model are rejected. If no data directly addresses the input question, the response will state “insufficient evidence” along with identifying the gap and suggesting the experiment that would provide the answer.

Benefits and impact

Based on NASA’s SAME experiment on the ISS under the studied conditions, researchers determined that the tested smoke detector would have remained below the alarm level in approximately two-thirds of Teflon smoke experiments and over half of Kapton smoke experiments. This information is dispersed across various databases and research papers. With Silent Alarm, all of this information is compiled into one place; each piece of evidence still includes its limitations, and the data directly shows that these records contain no smoke detector experiments at either Moon or Mars gravity. This helps directly indicate what experiments should still be performed as astronauts prepare for the Moon.

How it is creative

Other AI tools attempt to respond to any prompt. When evidence is lacking, Silent Alarm states this and suggests a future experiment as a response. In this way, “we don’t know” becomes a type of response.

Factors we considered

Trust: Responses are only provided if they reference NASA data

Accuracy: All assertions include their study-specific qualifier and source

Security: API key remains on the server

Accessibility: Responsive on mobile devices, uses high-contrast text and is keyboard navigable

Honesty regarding capabilities: Only states what its records cover

Tools used

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python (AWS Lambda), AWS Amplify, Groq (gpt-oss-120b), Transformers.js (MiniLM), GitHub. AI was used to generate the team logo.
